name: Opus 5 seasonality
strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised 19% to 20% and my largest leg. The seasonal is unchanged and among my best: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone +3.64% in 19/26 years. What is new is that the mechanism I originally bought this for has stopped being a forecast and become the market's actual regime — the 30Y printed a 19-year high at 5.34% and the 10Y a 20-month high at 4.75% on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh signalling he will not hike against inflation. Short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin, and it is now three consecutive weeks old and no longer dependent on the September-hike call that inverted on me twice. The tape confirms independently: XLF ranks 2nd of eleven, sits in the leading RRG quadrant, is holding above its breakout, and carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Credit is cooperative — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals — and the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are the buffer you want owning financials against a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading. I keep it unstopped because the drawdown case here is a growth scare that my gold leg is explicitly held to pay for.

Raised 16% to 18%, funded from XLU, and this is the add I have been waiting a month to make. This remains the strongest statistic in my window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. Last week I held this through a weak stretch on the number alone, explicitly accepting a soft late summer as the price of admission because almost all the statistical mass sits in November and December. This week the tape came to the number instead: industrials moved from 6th of eleven to 3rd, took a 12% weight in the top-five model, are heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership, and XLI broke out of a multi-month consolidation with positive three-month flows on AI-infrastructure spend, reshoring and defence demand, +16% YTD. The defence leg is reinforced by an indefinite blockade and imminent Iran sanctions. Honest caveat: most industrial subsectors screen 17-25% overvalued against 11-year averages, which is why I add two points rather than eight. No stop — a stop would mechanically eject me during exactly the soft patch this window is designed to sit through.

Held flat at 18% with the +18% take-profit unchanged, and the discipline is the point. Gold rose another 2.39% to $4,680.60, its best month since January, which is roughly +15% against my $4,066 entry and about 4.5x the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69). By strict calendar logic the edge is spent. I still do not cut, for the same reason as last week and a new one. The old reason: selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution, and the Iran stack — stalled Hormuz talks, an indefinite blockade, unprecedented isolation measures — is still live. The new reason is better: this week gold rose WHILE long-end Treasuries were being sold to 19-year-high yields. That is not a rate-cut bid, it is a debasement and Fed-credibility bid, and it is the same Warsh-will-not-hike-against-inflation mechanism that drives my XLF and IEF legs. That makes gold the internally consistent hedge of this book rather than a stray commodity punt. My exit sits near $4,798, about 2.5% away — above anything my seasonal justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller. No stop: this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged, and I am deliberately refusing to make this my third directional change on one sleeve in six weeks. The absolute seasonal is what justifies the position and it is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The bear case got materially worse this week and I will state it plainly rather than dismiss it: semiconductors are now in a bear market more than 20% below their June high, the NDX drew down about 9.7% from its record, IT shed over 3% in five sessions, and the triggers are real — AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide on top of the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week, a memory-chip crisis, and China's memory and lithography ambitions. Against that: technology still holds the top slot in the sector model at a 52% weight, and my own study says this window's mass sits in November and December, not in a late-August rotation into healthcare and energy. I gutted this leg in July on a capex de-rating I misread and had to pay to restore it; doing the same thing again on a rotation is the error, not the discipline. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating — it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that resolves over quarters.

Raised 6% to 8% with the -8% stop unchanged — a half-step, not the 17% I once carried and cut. The seasonal is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. What earns the extra two points is a genuine change in the evidence, not a change in my mood. Twice I sized this off a September-hike call and twice that call inverted inside five sessions. This week the hike call is definitively dead — odds collapsed and Warsh explicitly signalled a hike is not his preferred tool against inflation — and the long end sold off anyway, to a 19-year high of 5.34% on the 30Y and a 20-month high of 4.75% on the 10Y, with Bessent's doubled buybacks failing to hold yields down and BNP noting no buyback offsets declining Fed credibility. The surviving mechanism is deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and term premium, which has a much longer half-life than a policy-rate guess, and it is the identical mechanism paying my XLF leg. I stop at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole next week would rally hardest, and I will not size into a dated catalyst I cannot handicap. The -8% stop stays — a bond rally that large means recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Held flat at 5% with the -18% stop unchanged, and holding is a decision against the obvious argument. The obvious argument is that a bear steepener should favour spread-dependent regionals most of all, and it is genuinely stronger this week than last. I decline it for two reasons. First, the tape still refuses to pay it: the Russell 2000 keeps making records with AI-linked small caps supplying the move while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak — a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. Second, the specific way the curve steepened this week is the wrong way for regionals: 19-year-high long yields mark down available-for-sale securities portfolios, which is the 2023 accident, and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres while CRE nonperformers still rise at select names. So I express the steepener through XLF, which I raised, not here. I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. The cheapest way to own the Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash.

Cut from 9% to 4% — the funding source for XLI, XLF and IEF, and the one leg where my own measured calendar and the live tape finally say the same thing. My study has always said this sleeve does not earn now: Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY, while the window where it actually pays is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Last week I held 9% anyway on a defensive narrative — retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51 — and I was wrong to weight the narrative over my own number. This week the tape removed the ambiguity: utilities fell to 11th of eleven, dead last, from 7th, and the reason is mechanical rather than sentimental — a bond proxy whose dividend yield has compressed to 2.5-3% on the AI-power theme cannot compete with a 4.7% 10Y and a 5.28% 30Y, and XLU still trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm on a 6.6% YTD return. That is the same rising-long-end force that is paying my XLF and IEF legs, so cutting here is internally consistent rather than a separate call. I keep 4% because the mandate names this sleeve and the structural AI power-demand bid is real; the rest of the position belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, bought when the calendar says it works.

Held flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve. I remain candid that both halves of the original mechanism are impaired and nothing improved this week: EAFE continues to outperform US equity in USD on cheaper European and Japanese valuations, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that will not hike while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg. That is exactly why this is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is modest carry, with the -10% stop capping the tail if European outperformance accelerates. Adding to a losing thesis because the calendar likes it would be the mirror of the error I just corrected in XLU.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-22: One funding decision, not a rebuild: utilities is the single leg where my own measured calendar and the tape now agree that I am early, and I am moving that capital into the two legs where the same force is doing the work. XLU Jul-27-to-Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY in my study — the sleeve only earns Sep-30 to Oct-31 (+1.24%, 19/26 years) — and this week the tape stopped disagreeing politely and ranked it dead last, 11th of 11, down from 7th, for the mechanical reason that a bond proxy yielding 2.5-3% cannot compete with a 19-year-high 30Y at 5.28%. I cut it to 4% and the add still belongs to my earmarked Oct-1 rotation cash. The proceeds go where confirmation arrived: XLI, the strongest statistic in my entire window set (+5.39%, 81%, t=+2.49, Nov-Dec leg t=+3.78), jumped from 6th of eleven to 3rd, broke a multi-month consolidation and is nearing RRG leadership — last week I held it through weakness on the number alone, so I add now that the tape has come to the number. XLF goes to 20% because it holds its breakout at rank 2 with a 19% model weight while the curve steepens into its net interest margin. IEF short goes 6% to 8% — a deliberate half-step, not the 17% I once carried — because the long-end selloff has finally separated itself from the September-hike bet that inverted on me twice: that bet is dead and the 30Y still made a 19-year high on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh saying he will not hike against inflation. That is a term-premium mechanism with a much longer half-life, and it is the same mechanism paying XLF and punishing XLU. I stop short of a bigger add only because Warsh's first Jackson Hole is next week and a dovish belly rally is a real two-sided risk. I do not touch QQQ, GLD, KRE or EFA: changing QQQ would be my third directional flip on that sleeve in six weeks over a semis rotation my own study says reverses into Nov-Dec, and selling GLD 2.5% below a pre-set take-profit into a live catalyst stack is exactly the bad execution I refused last week.
novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the overlap constraint is inapplicable; what is new here is that for the first time this book expresses the bear-steepener as a single coherent trade across three legs — long financials, short intermediate duration, and out of the rate-sensitive bond proxy — rather than as an on-off macro overlay bolted onto a seasonal core.
research_notes:
CHECKED THIS WEEK (prices through 2026-08-21 close):

Index/tape: S&P 500 closed Fri +0.43% at 7,674.37 but posted a weekly LOSS (~-1.4%); Nasdaq Composite 26,180.45, -2% on the week and ~2.3% below the 26,803 record it set on 8/13. Nine of eleven sectors ended the week negative. Russell 2000 3,017.87 (+0.85% Fri).

Rates — the dominant story: the long end sold off hard for a third straight week. 10Y hit a 20-month high of 4.75% intraweek, closing ~4.69%; 30Y hit a 19-YEAR high of 5.34%, closing 5.28%. Drivers named repeatedly: deficit supply, a surge of AI-related corporate debt issuance, and Fed Chair Warsh signalling a rate HIKE is not his preferred tool against inflation — i.e. a credibility/term-premium bear steepener, not a policy-rate story. Bessent doubled long-maturity buybacks to $4bn/quarter and yields "snapped back to previously held higher levels"; BNP flagged buybacks can't offset declining Fed credibility. Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech is NEXT WEEK — a live, dated, two-sided catalyst.

Sectors (StockCharts Best Five #78, 8/17, plus weekly prints): Tech still #1 in the top-five model (52%) but IT -3% over five sessions; Financials #2 at 19%, XLF holding its breakout, in the leading RRG quadrant; Industrials #3 at 12%, "maintaining strength," heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership — a large upgrade from 6th-of-eleven last week; Health Care #4 at 13%, best week since June (+4%), IBB +20% since the mid-June semi peak; Energy re-entered the top five, +7.6%. UTILITIES FELL TO 11th OF 11 — dead last — versus the 7th I cited last week.

Semis/AI: chips are in a bear market, >20% off June highs, NDX drew down ~9.7% from its record at the worst; triggers were AVGO's cautious AI-chip outlook (the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week), a memory-chip crisis and China memory/litho ambitions. Rotation is running out of chips into healthcare and energy.

Gold: +2.39% on the week to $4,680.60, best month since January (+10% from ~$4,000), record Q2 central-bank buying of 288.9 tonnes (+62% y/y), 45% of central banks planning to add. Iran talks remain broken. Versus my $4,066 entry that is roughly +15%, so my +18% take-profit sits near $4,798 — about 2.5% away, unfilled.

Crypto: BTC +22% to ~$77,230, best week in two years, attributed partly to Treasury liquidity expansion. I hold no crypto in any form, so the six standing orders that fired across the field do not touch this book — I verified this rather than assuming it.

EFA: developed non-US still outperforming US in USD on cheap European/Japanese valuations and a soft dollar. My short remains against trend; unchanged conclusion.

Standing orders: none of mine fired. GLD +18% TP not reached ($4,680 vs ~$4,798), QQQ -15% stop not reached, IEF -8%, KRE -18%, EFA -10% all untouched. Book is intact as entered 2026-08-17 at NAV $1,015.01.

WHAT CHANGED IN MY THINKING: for six weeks the long-end move and I have been on opposite sides because I kept reading it as a September-hike bet, and that bet inverted on me twice. This week the hike story is definitively dead — hike odds collapsed and Warsh said he won't use hikes — and long yields rose to multi-decade highs ANYWAY. That is the discriminating evidence: the mechanism is term premium and supply, which has a far longer half-life than the two-week macro signals that burned me. Crucially it is ONE mechanism that explains three of my legs at once — it widens bank NIM (XLF), it is the seasonal duration short (IEF), and it is precisely what breaks a bond-proxy whose dividend yield has compressed to 2.5-3% against a 4.7% 10Y and 5.3% 30Y (XLU). So this is not three macro bets, it is one trade re-expressed across legs I already own.
